quote: I got the bill the electricity bill of men for $700.
stewart_read: The customer hands over a striking, specific bill figure ($700, later $580, $520, $480) unprompted. The rep never reflects this back, never asks what she'd want the bill to look like, and never uses it to build curiosity about a new/fixed system — it's simply filed as color while the call pivots to ownership questions.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may have judged the existing-system complication made bill-anchoring premature since Ion may not be able to help at all — a reasonable reactive triage call, but not one supported by an explicit rep statement.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to acknowledge big bill numbers explicitly ('$700 in one month is rough') even in orphaned-system calls — it costs nothing and keeps the door open if the existing system turns out to be unserviceable or she wants a second system evaluated.

quote: do you, do you know who you are, like, who the solar is with at all? Like, when you when you bought the house?
stewart_read: This is the correct first move for an orphaned-system scenario, but the rep stops at one question instead of running the fuller orphaned_flow checklist (own vs. lease, company name, panel size, working status) that would let a closer or the rep make a real determination.
alternative_hypothesis: Reactive read: rep simply forgot the rest of the orphaned checklist. Strategic read would require evidence the rep deliberately triaged to end the call quickly, which isn't supported here — the rep kept trying to help via repeated disclaimers.
coaching_implication: Walk the rep through the full orphaned_flow question set so a callback isn't the only outcome available on these calls.

quote: The issue is is we won't be able to do anything on equipment that might not be our own.
stewart_read: Correct substantive answer (Ion can't service someone else's install), but delivered as a full stop rather than a bridge — no attempt to ask if she'd be interested in an additional/expanded system, or to flag the account for a callback with a specific time.
alternative_hypothesis: Could be read as protocol discipline (accurately declining to service equipment Ion didn't install) rather than a gap — the substance of the answer is correct.
coaching_implication: Keep the accurate disclaimer, but pair it with a forward-looking question: is she interested in solar generally if this system turns out to be a dead end, or if it needs replacing.

quote: Give me can can I I'm sorry. I'm sorry. Can I have ten seconds? I just need to see who's calling me.
stewart_read: Customer steps away for what becomes roughly a 40-second gap (02:53 to 03:55) to check another incoming call; the rep holds the line silently. This isn't a rep-caused issue but is worth noting as dead air that the rep did nothing to fill or use (e.g., no follow-up question queued for when she returned).
coaching_implication: Minor — no action needed beyond noting the rep handled the interruption patiently and picked the conversation back up without losing the customer.

quote: Yes. I again, I would just figure out who you, who the solar would is with. Because if it is us, then we can definitely take a look at it.
stewart_read: After the roof-call interruption, the rep repeats the identical disclaimer almost word-for-word instead of trying a different angle — e.g., referencing her own $700 bill again, or asking if she'd want a second opinion on a new system regardless of the existing one's status.
alternative_hypothesis: This could be read as appropriate consistency/protocol discipline rather than a failure of resilience, since the underlying fact (Ion can't service others' equipment) hasn't changed.
coaching_implication: Encourage the rep to vary the follow-up even when the core answer stays the same — repeat the answer, but change the bridge or next-step each time to avoid sounding like a script loop.

quote: Yeah. Definitely give us a callback if it is our system, and then we can get you helped out. But, yeah, in the meantime, I'll I'll take you off the list so we're not on the bottom of your calls.
stewart_read: The call ends with no locked time, no rep-owned next step, and the rep actively offers to remove her from the call list rather than securing any commitment — functionally closing the door rather than keeping it open.
alternative_hypothesis: Could be read as considerate customer service (reducing unwanted calls) rather than a failure, but it removes Ion's ability to follow up proactively on a lead with a documented $700 bill.
coaching_implication: Even on an orphaned/DQ-adjacent call, avoid removing the customer from future outreach entirely — instead offer a specific callback window or note to re-contact in a set number of weeks.

quote: Okay. I'm a call I'm a save the number, and I'll call you back when I have my husband answer.
stewart_read: The customer references her husband as the one with the ownership/purchase details ('my man did the did that... he said he still had to pay some money for the solar panel'), and ends the call planning to involve him — but the rep never proactively suggests a joint callback time or offers to coordinate with the husband directly.
alternative_hypothesis: Reactive read: rep missed the chance to lock a joint callback. Strategic read: since the call was heading toward a likely non-serviceable orphaned system, scheduling firmly may have been premature — but even so, a suggested day/time would have been low-cost and consistent with protocol.
coaching_implication: When a co-decider is referenced as the fact-holder, propose a specific callback time to reach both of them, rather than leaving it entirely to the customer to initiate.
